title: Rights, Courts and Taking Part
bigQuestion: What rights do you have right now, how did people win them, and what can you do with them before you are old enough to vote?

story.title: Two Inches of Black Cloth
story.kicker: In December 1965, a thirteen-year-old in Des Moines pinned a strip of black cloth to her sleeve and started a case that still protects students today.
paragraphs: In December 1965, the war in Vietnam was growing, and so were the protests against it. In Des Moines, Iowa, a small group of families decided to mourn the dead on both sides by wearing black armbands during the holidays. Among them were Mary Beth Tinker, who was thirteen and in eighth grade, her brother John, who was fifteen, and their friend Christopher Eckhardt, who was sixteen. They were not planning a march or a walkout. They planned to sit in class with two inches of black cloth on one arm.

The school principals heard about the plan two days early. They met and passed a rule: any student wearing an armband would be asked to remove it, and any who refused would be suspended. The students knew about the rule and wore the armbands anyway. Mary Beth wore hers to math class. A teacher sent her to the office. She was suspended, and so were John and Christopher and two others. They stayed home until after New Year's Day, when the protest was scheduled to end.

The students' parents believed the school had broken the First Amendment, which protects freedom of speech. With help from a civil liberties group, they sued the school district in federal court. They lost. The judge said the school had acted reasonably to prevent a disturbance. They appealed and lost again, on a tie vote. Then they asked the Supreme Court of the United States to hear the case. It agreed. Three years after the armbands, the Tinkers walked into the marble courtroom in Washington.

The school's lawyers argued that schools must keep order, and that a symbol of protest could set off fights. The students' lawyer pointed out that other students had worn political buttons and even the Iron Cross, a German military symbol, without being punished. Only the armbands were banned. The school had not been protecting order. It had been silencing one opinion it did not like.

On February 24, 1969, the Court ruled seven to two for the students. Justice Abe Fortas wrote that students do not shed their constitutional rights to freedom of speech or expression at the schoolhouse gate. Schools could limit speech that substantially disrupted learning, but a quiet armband was not that. Mary Beth Tinker grew up to be a nurse and still visits schools to talk about the case. The rule from her case is the reason you can wear a message on your shirt tomorrow, as long as it does not disrupt class.
story.think: The school said it was keeping order. The students said it was silencing an opinion. How could a judge tell the difference? What evidence mattered most?

lessons.title: Why the First Ten Amendments Exist
lessons.mainIdea: The Bill of Rights was added in 1791 to list the freedoms the new government could not take away.
reading: When the Constitution went to the states for approval in 1787, many people refused to support it. Their objection was simple. The document said what the government could do, but it did not say what the government could never do to the people. Where was the promise of free speech, or a fair trial? Some states approved the Constitution only after being promised that a list of rights would be added. James Madison, who had once thought such a list unnecessary, wrote one.

The first ten *amendments*, approved by the states in 1791, are called the *Bill of Rights*. Each one is a fence around the government. The First Amendment alone protects five freedoms: religion, speech, the press, peaceful assembly, and petition, which means asking the government to fix a wrong. Notice how it begins: Congress shall make no law. The amendment does not give you the right to speak. It assumes you already have it and forbids the government from taking it.

Free speech protects speech you hate as well as speech you love. In 1977 a small group of American Nazis planned a march in Skokie, a Chicago suburb where thousands of survivors of the Holocaust lived. The village tried to block the march. Courts, including the Illinois Supreme Court, ruled that the village could not ban a march because of its message, no matter how hateful. The group ended up marching in Chicago instead. Many people found the ruling painful. That was the point: rights that protect only popular ideas protect no one.

The freedoms of the First Amendment have limits. You cannot shout a false alarm that causes a stampede, threaten to hurt someone, or print a lie that ruins a person's business. Schools can stop speech that disrupts learning. But the burden is on the government to prove why speech must be limited, not on you to prove why you may speak. That order of proof is what makes the amendment powerful.

words.d: official changes or additions to the Constitution
the first ten amendments to the Constitution, approved in 1791, which list protected freedoms
to formally ask the government to fix a problem or change a policy

look.title: The First Amendment
look.text: Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof; or abridging the freedom of speech, or of the press; or the right of the people peaceably to assemble, and to petition the Government for a redress of grievances.
look.cite: First Amendment to the United States Constitution, ratified 1791
look.prompt: Find the five freedoms in this sentence. Which one do you use most often, and which one have you never used?

check.q: Why did some states refuse to approve the Constitution at first?
choices: It made the president too weak
It did not list the rights the government could never take away
It gave too much power to the states
It had no preamble
check.why: Critics wanted a written list of protected freedoms. Several states approved the Constitution only after being promised one.

check.q: Which freedom is NOT one of the five in the First Amendment?
choices: Freedom of the press
Freedom to petition
Freedom to own a gun
Freedom of religion
check.why: The First Amendment protects religion, speech, the press, assembly and petition. The right to bear arms is in the Second Amendment.

check.q: What did courts decide about the planned Nazi march in Skokie in 1977?
choices: The march could be banned because its message was hateful
The village could charge the marchers a large fee
The marchers had to get permission from Congress
The village could not ban a march because of its message
check.why: Courts ruled that even hateful speech is protected from government bans based on its message, though many people found the decision painful.

lessons.title: Arms, Soldiers and Searches
lessons.mainIdea: The Second, Third and Fourth Amendments limit what the government can do with weapons, soldiers and searches.
reading: The *Second Amendment* protects the right to keep and bear arms. It is one sentence long and mentions a well regulated militia, which in 1791 meant ordinary citizens who could be called up to defend a town. Americans have argued for two centuries about whether the amendment protects a personal right or only a militia's. In 2008 the Supreme Court ruled that it protects an individual right to keep a handgun at home, while allowing many laws about who may own guns and where they may be carried.

The Third Amendment says the government cannot force you to house soldiers in your home in peacetime. Before the Revolution, British troops had been quartered in colonists' houses, and the memory stung. Today the amendment is almost never used in court. It matters mostly as a reminder that your home is yours, an idea the Fourth Amendment builds on.

The *Fourth Amendment* protects people against unreasonable searches and seizures. Police normally need a *warrant*, a written order from a judge, to search your home, and to get one they must show probable cause, meaning good reason to believe evidence of a crime is there. Evidence found in an illegal search usually cannot be used at trial. That rule gives police a strong reason to follow the law.

At school, the rule is looser. In 1985 the Supreme Court decided a case about a New Jersey student whose purse was searched after she was caught smoking. The Court ruled that school officials need only reasonable suspicion, not a warrant, because schools must keep students safe. Lockers are usually school property and can be searched. Your phone is a harder question that courts are still working out. Knowing the rule is the first step to knowing when it has been broken.

words.d: the amendment that protects the right to keep and bear arms
the amendment that protects against unreasonable searches and seizures
a written order from a judge that allows police to search a place or arrest a person
a good reason, based on facts, to believe a crime was committed or evidence is present

look.title: The Locker and the Backpack
look.text: A principal gets a tip that a student has a knife. She opens the student's locker without asking. She finds nothing. Then she asks to look in the student's backpack. The student says no. The principal looks anyway and finds a knife.
look.prompt: Which search seems fair to you, and why? What does the school gain by having a lower standard than the police, and what do students lose?

check.q: What must police normally show a judge to get a search warrant?
choices: A confession
A witness who saw the crime
Probable cause that evidence of a crime is there
Permission from the mayor
check.why: A warrant requires probable cause: real facts that give good reason to believe evidence of a crime will be found.

check.q: Why does the Third Amendment exist?
choices: To let soldiers vote
To protect the right to own weapons
To keep the army small
Because British troops had been forced into colonists' homes
check.why: The colonists resented being made to house British soldiers, so the amendment bans forced quartering in peacetime.

check.q: How is a search at school different from a police search?
choices: School officials need only reasonable suspicion, not a warrant
Schools can never search students
Schools need a warrant from the school board
Schools must search every student equally
check.why: The Supreme Court ruled in 1985 that schools need only reasonable suspicion because they must keep students safe.

lessons.title: Rights of the Accused
lessons.mainIdea: The Fifth through Eighth Amendments protect anyone accused of a crime, whether guilty or innocent.
reading: The framers knew that a government can crush a person by accusing them of a crime. So four amendments protect the accused. The *Fifth Amendment* says you cannot be tried twice for the same crime, which is called double jeopardy. It says you cannot be forced to be a witness against yourself, which is where the phrase taking the Fifth comes from. And it says no one can lose life, liberty or property without *due process* of law, meaning fair procedures that follow known rules.

The Sixth Amendment lists what a fair criminal trial includes: it must be speedy and public, decided by an impartial jury, and the accused must be told the charges, may confront the witnesses, and may have a lawyer. In 1963, a Florida man named Clarence Gideon, too poor to hire a lawyer, wrote to the Supreme Court in pencil from his prison cell. The Court ruled that states must provide a lawyer to anyone accused of a serious crime who cannot afford one. Public defenders in every Illinois county exist because of that letter.

The Seventh Amendment guarantees a jury in many civil cases, which are disputes between people over money or property rather than crimes. The *Eighth Amendment* bans excessive bail, excessive fines, and cruel and unusual punishments. What counts as cruel has changed over time. In 2005 the Supreme Court ruled that no one can be executed for a crime committed before age eighteen. Illinois ended the death penalty entirely in 2011, after a series of innocent men were found on its death row.

These rights protect the guilty as well as the innocent, and that bothers some people. But think about why they exist. The government has police, prosecutors and prisons. An accused person often has nothing. The amendments even the contest a little. A rule that protected only the innocent would be useless, because the whole point of a trial is that we do not yet know who is innocent.

words.d: the amendment that protects against double jeopardy and self-incrimination and guarantees due process
fair legal procedures that the government must follow before taking away life, liberty or property
the amendment that bans excessive bail, excessive fines and cruel and unusual punishment

look.title: A Letter in Pencil
look.text: Clarence Gideon was accused of breaking into a pool hall in Florida in 1961. He asked the judge for a lawyer and was told the state did not provide one for his kind of case. He defended himself, lost, and got five years. From prison he wrote to the Supreme Court in pencil, arguing that a trial without a lawyer was not fair. The Court agreed. At his second trial, with a lawyer, a jury found him not guilty.
look.prompt: Why might the same facts produce a guilty verdict without a lawyer and a not guilty verdict with one? What does that say about how much a trial depends on the lawyer?

check.q: What does the Fifth Amendment's protection against double jeopardy mean?
choices: You cannot be searched twice
You cannot be tried twice for the same crime
You cannot be fined more than twice
Two judges must agree on a verdict
check.why: Double jeopardy means being put on trial again for the same crime after a verdict, and the Fifth Amendment forbids it.

check.q: What did the Supreme Court decide in Clarence Gideon's case in 1963?
choices: That juries must be unanimous
That the death penalty is cruel
That states must provide a lawyer to poor people accused of serious crimes
That trials must be public
check.why: Gideon's pencil letter led to the rule that anyone accused of a serious crime who cannot afford a lawyer must be given one.

check.q: Why do the rights of the accused protect guilty people as well as innocent ones?
choices: Because judges cannot tell the difference
Because the framers wanted fewer convictions
Because guilty people have more rights
Because at the start of a trial no one yet knows who is innocent
check.why: A trial exists to find out who is guilty. Rules that applied only to the innocent would be impossible to apply before the verdict.

lessons.title: Freedom, Citizenship and the Vote
lessons.mainIdea: The Thirteenth, Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendments ended slavery and promised citizenship and the vote to Black Americans.
reading: The Bill of Rights of 1791 was written for a country where about seven hundred thousand people were enslaved, and it did nothing for them. By 1860 the number was about four million. It took the Civil War, which killed more than six hundred thousand soldiers, to change the Constitution. The *Thirteenth Amendment*, ratified in 1865, abolished slavery everywhere in the United States. Illinois was the first state to ratify it, on February 1, 1865, the day after Congress passed it, urged on by Abraham Lincoln.

Freedom without rights was not enough. Southern states passed laws that kept formerly enslaved people from owning land, testifying in court or moving freely. So in 1868 the *Fourteenth Amendment* declared that everyone born in the United States is a citizen. It ordered that no state may deny any person the equal protection of the laws or take life, liberty or property without due process. For the first time, the Constitution's promises bound the states, not just Congress.

The *Fifteenth Amendment*, ratified in 1870, said the right to vote could not be denied because of race, color, or having once been enslaved. For a few years Black men voted and were elected across the South. Then the promise was broken. States invented poll taxes, reading tests and violence to keep Black citizens from the polls. It took nearly a century, the Voting Rights Act of 1965, and the courage of ordinary people to make the Fifteenth Amendment real.

The Fourteenth Amendment turned out to be the most powerful sentence in the Constitution. Its words equal protection have been used to end school segregation, to protect immigrants, and to strike down laws that treated women differently from men. When someone in Illinois argues today that a law treats one group unfairly, they are almost always standing on the Fourteenth Amendment. It was written for freed people. It ended up protecting everyone.

words.d: the 1865 amendment that abolished slavery in the United States
the 1868 amendment that made everyone born in the United States a citizen and promised equal protection of the laws
the 1870 amendment that said the right to vote cannot be denied because of race
the rule that a government must treat people in the same situation the same way

look.title: When Rights Were Added
look.prompt: Find the longest gap between two amendments on this list. What was happening during those years that might explain the wait?

check.q: What did the Fourteenth Amendment do that the original Bill of Rights did not?
choices: It made the Constitution's promises bind the states, not just Congress
It created the Supreme Court
It gave women the vote
It ended the Civil War
check.why: The Bill of Rights limited only Congress. The Fourteenth Amendment ordered the states to give due process and equal protection.

check.q: Which state was the first to ratify the Thirteenth Amendment?
choices: Massachusetts
Illinois
New York
Virginia
check.why: Illinois ratified on February 1, 1865, the day after Congress passed the amendment, with President Lincoln urging it on.

check.q: Why did the Fifteenth Amendment fail to protect Black voters for nearly a century?
choices: It was never ratified
It applied only to Northern states
States used poll taxes, reading tests and violence to keep Black citizens from voting
It expired after ten years
check.why: The amendment was law, but states found ways around it until the Voting Rights Act of 1965 and the civil rights movement forced change.

lessons.title: Women and Young Voters
lessons.mainIdea: The Nineteenth and Twenty-Sixth Amendments extended the vote to women and to citizens as young as eighteen.
reading: In 1848, a group of women and men met in Seneca Falls, New York, and declared that women should have the vote. It took seventy-two years. Women marched, gave speeches, were arrested, and in some cases went on hunger strikes in jail. Some states let women vote early; Wyoming did it in 1869. In Illinois, a 1913 law let women vote for president and for many local offices, the first such law east of the Mississippi River. That put Illinois women at the polls seven years before most of the country.

The *Nineteenth Amendment*, ratified in 1920, said the right to vote could not be denied on account of sex. Illinois was among the very first states to ratify it, in June 1919. The amendment did not fix everything. Black women in the South were still blocked by the same tricks used against Black men, and Native American women were often not counted as citizens until 1924. But the number of American voters roughly doubled, and every election since has been shaped by it.

The *Twenty-Sixth Amendment* came from a war. During the Vietnam War, men could be drafted into the army at eighteen but could not vote until twenty-one. The slogan was old enough to fight, old enough to vote. Congress passed the amendment in March 1971, and the states ratified it in about three months, faster than any amendment before or since. If you are eighteen on election day, that amendment is why you can vote.

Look at the pattern in these amendments. None of them says who may vote. Each says who may not be kept from voting: not because of race, not because of sex, not because of age over eighteen. The Constitution grew by removing barriers one at a time, each one after a long fight by the people the barrier kept out. Some Illinois towns now let sixteen-year-olds vote in local elections in other states, and some students argue Illinois should try it too.

words.d: the 1920 amendment that said the right to vote cannot be denied on account of sex
the 1971 amendment that set the voting age at eighteen
the right to vote

look.title: The Nineteenth Amendment
look.text: The right of citizens of the United States to vote shall not be denied or abridged by the United States or by any State on account of sex.
look.cite: Nineteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution, ratified 1920
look.prompt: The amendment does not say women may vote. It says the vote may not be denied on account of sex. Why might the writers have chosen that wording?

check.q: What did Illinois do in 1913?
choices: Elected a woman governor
Ratified the Nineteenth Amendment
Lowered the voting age to eighteen
Let women vote for president and many local offices, before most of the country
check.why: A 1913 Illinois law gave women a partial vote, the first such law east of the Mississippi, seven years before the Nineteenth Amendment.

check.q: What argument drove the Twenty-Sixth Amendment?
choices: People who are old enough to be drafted are old enough to vote
Eighteen-year-olds pay more taxes
Colleges wanted more students to vote
The Supreme Court ordered it
check.why: During the Vietnam War, men could be drafted at eighteen but not vote until twenty-one. The amendment closed that gap in 1971.

check.q: What pattern do the voting amendments share?
choices: Each one names a group that must vote
Each one removes a reason the vote can be denied
Each one was ratified in less than a year
Each one applied only to federal elections
check.why: The amendments do not grant the vote. They forbid denying it on account of race, sex or age over eighteen.

lessons.title: How a Court Case Works
lessons.mainIdea: A case moves from a trial court through appeals, and only a few reach the Supreme Court.
reading: There are two kinds of cases. A *criminal case* is brought by the government against someone accused of breaking a law, and the punishment can be prison. A *civil case* is a dispute between people or groups over money, property or rights, and the result is usually an order to pay or to stop doing something. The Tinker case was civil: the students were not accused of a crime. They were asking a court to order the school to stop punishing them.

A case begins in a trial court. The person who brings a civil case is the *plaintiff*, and the person being sued is the *defendant*. Each side presents evidence and witnesses. A jury, or sometimes a judge alone, decides the facts. The judge applies the law. The loser can *appeal*, asking a higher court to check whether the trial court made a legal mistake. Appeals courts do not hold new trials or hear witnesses. They read the record and the lawyers' written arguments.

Above the appeals courts sits a supreme court, either the Illinois Supreme Court for state law or the United States Supreme Court for federal law. The U.S. Supreme Court chooses which cases to take, and it takes very few. It usually picks cases where lower courts disagree or where a big question about the Constitution needs an answer. Nine justices hear the lawyers argue for about an hour, then vote in private.

One justice writes the majority opinion, which explains the decision and becomes the rule for every court below. Justices who disagree write a *dissent*. Dissents do not win, but they matter. Justice John Marshall Harlan's lone dissent in 1896, when the Court approved separate railroad cars for Black and white passengers, argued that the Constitution is color-blind. Fifty-eight years later, his view became the law. A case name like Tinker v. Des Moines means Tinker against Des Moines; the v. is short for versus.

words.d: a case brought by the government against a person accused of breaking a law
a dispute between people or groups over money, property or rights
the person who brings a civil case to court
a request that a higher court review a lower court's decision for legal mistakes
a written opinion by justices who disagree with the majority's decision

look.title: Three Years, Three Courts
look.text: The Tinkers lost in a federal district court in Iowa in 1966. They lost again in a court of appeals in 1967, when the judges split evenly. They won in the Supreme Court in 1969. The armbands had been worn for about a week. The lawsuit lasted more than three years, and by the end Mary Beth was in high school.
look.prompt: Why does the system let a case go through so many courts? Who benefits from the slowness, and who pays for it?

check.q: What is the difference between a criminal case and a civil case?
choices: Criminal cases are heard only by the Supreme Court
Civil cases always involve a jury
A criminal case is brought by the government and can lead to prison, while a civil case is a dispute between people or groups
Civil cases are about violent crimes
check.why: The government prosecutes crimes. Civil cases, like the Tinkers' lawsuit, are disputes over money, property or rights.

check.q: What does an appeals court do?
choices: Holds a new trial with new witnesses
Decides whether the person is guilty
Chooses the jury
Reviews whether the trial court made a legal mistake
check.why: Appeals courts read the record and the lawyers' arguments to check for legal errors. They do not retry the facts.

check.q: Why can a dissent matter even though it loses?
choices: Its reasoning can become the law years later
It cancels the majority opinion
It forces a new trial
It is the only opinion that lower courts must follow
check.why: Justice Harlan's 1896 dissent that the Constitution is color-blind lost, but its view became the law in 1954.

lessons.title: Brown: Separate Is Not Equal
lessons.mainIdea: In 1954 the Supreme Court ruled that segregated public schools violate the Fourteenth Amendment.
reading: In Topeka, Kansas, in 1951, a third grader named Linda Brown walked past a white elementary school near her home to catch a bus to a Black school across town. Her father, Oliver Brown, joined a lawsuit with a dozen other families. The case joined others from South Carolina, Virginia, Delaware and Washington, D.C. Together they asked one question: does forcing Black children into separate schools violate the Fourteenth Amendment's promise of equal protection?

The law seemed to be against them. In 1896, in a case called Plessy v. Ferguson, the Supreme Court had ruled that separate facilities for Black and white people were legal as long as they were equal. In practice, they were never equal. Black schools in the South often had no heat, no buses and hand-me-down books. The lawyer for the families, Thurgood Marshall, showed the Court evidence of those gaps. He also showed studies suggesting that segregation itself made Black children feel inferior.

On May 17, 1954, the Court ruled unanimously, nine to zero, for the families. Chief Justice Earl Warren wrote that in public education, separate but equal has no place, because separate schools are inherently unequal. The decision did not end segregation overnight. Some Southern states resisted for years. In 1957 the president sent soldiers to Little Rock, Arkansas, to protect nine Black students entering a high school.

Brown mattered in Illinois too. The state had banned school segregation by law in 1874, but Chicago's schools were sharply divided by neighborhood, and in 1963 more than two hundred thousand students stayed home for one day to protest overcrowded, underfunded Black schools. Brown gave protesters a tool: the Constitution now said what they had always known. Thurgood Marshall became the first Black justice of the Supreme Court in 1967.

words.d: separating people by race in schools, housing or public places
the 1896 Supreme Court case that allowed separate but equal facilities for Black and white people
agreed to by everyone; a nine-to-zero vote of the Supreme Court

look.title: Inherently Unequal
look.text: We conclude that in the field of public education the doctrine of 'separate but equal' has no place. Separate educational facilities are inherently unequal.
look.cite: Chief Justice Earl Warren, Brown v. Board of Education, 1954
look.prompt: Inherently means by its very nature. Why did the Court say separate schools could never be equal, even if the buildings and books were the same?

check.q: What had the Supreme Court ruled in Plessy v. Ferguson in 1896?
choices: That segregation was illegal everywhere
That separate facilities for Black and white people were legal if they were equal
That schools must be integrated within a year
That only Congress could decide on segregation
check.why: Plessy allowed separate but equal facilities, a rule the Court overturned for schools in Brown in 1954.

check.q: Who argued the Brown case for the families?
choices: Earl Warren
Oliver Brown
Thurgood Marshall
John Marshall Harlan
check.why: Thurgood Marshall argued the case and later became the first Black justice of the Supreme Court in 1967.

check.q: How did the Court vote in Brown v. Board of Education?
choices: Five to four
Seven to two
Six to three
Nine to zero, unanimously
check.why: Chief Justice Warren worked to get every justice to agree, so the decision would carry the full weight of the Court.

lessons.title: Tinker: Speech at the Schoolhouse Gate
lessons.mainIdea: Tinker v. Des Moines protects student speech unless it substantially disrupts school.
reading: The 1969 decision in Tinker v. Des Moines set the rule that still governs speech in your school. Students keep their First Amendment rights inside school, the Court said. A school may limit speech only when it can show that the speech would cause, or did cause, a *substantial disruption* of school work or would invade the rights of others. Fear that a message might cause trouble is not enough. The school must have real evidence.

The Court did not say students can say anything. Later cases drew lines. In 1986 the Court let a school punish a student for a speech full of sexual jokes at an assembly, because schools may teach civil behavior. In 1988 it ruled that a principal could remove articles from a school newspaper produced in a journalism class, because the paper was part of the school's own program. In 2021 the Court protected a cheerleader who posted a profane complaint about her team on a weekend, off campus.

Put the cases together and a pattern appears. Speech that is political, personal and peaceful, like an armband or a shirt with a slogan, gets strong protection. Speech that is lewd, that is part of a school activity, or that threatens or bullies someone gets much less. Off-campus speech on your own time is mostly your business, though threats and harassment are not protected anywhere.

The Tinker rule works only if students know it. A shirt supporting a candidate, a silent protest, a petition passed between classes: all are protected as long as they do not disrupt learning. If a school tells you to remove a message, you can ask, calmly, what disruption it caused. That question is the Tinker test, and you are allowed to ask it. Mary Beth Tinker was thirteen when she asked it.

words.d: the Tinker test: a school may limit speech only if it seriously interferes with school work or others' rights
the 1969 Supreme Court case that protected students' right to peaceful symbolic speech in school
expressing an idea through an action or object, like an armband, rather than words

look.title: At the Schoolhouse Gate
look.text: It can hardly be argued that either students or teachers shed their constitutional rights to freedom of speech or expression at the schoolhouse gate.
look.cite: Justice Abe Fortas, Tinker v. Des Moines Independent Community School District, 1969
look.prompt: Fortas includes teachers as well as students. What might a teacher be allowed to say under this rule, and what might a school still be able to limit?

check.q: Under Tinker, when may a school limit student speech?
choices: When the school can show it would substantially disrupt school work or invade others' rights
Whenever the principal disagrees with the message
Only when the speech is about politics
Never, under any circumstances
check.why: The Tinker test requires evidence of real disruption, not just fear of trouble, before a school may limit speech.

check.q: Why could a principal remove articles from a school newspaper in the 1988 case?
choices: Because students have no press rights
Because the newspaper was part of the school's own class and program
Because the articles were political
Because the students wore armbands
check.why: The Court treated a class-produced paper as part of the school's program, which the school may control, unlike a student's personal speech.

check.q: Which of these would most likely be protected under the Tinker rule?
choices: A threat written on a locker
A speech full of sexual jokes at an assembly
A quiet shirt supporting a candidate
Bullying messages sent to a classmate
check.why: Peaceful political expression like a slogan shirt is protected unless it disrupts learning. Threats, lewd speech and bullying are not.

lessons.title: Miranda: You Have the Right
lessons.mainIdea: Miranda v. Arizona requires police to tell suspects their rights before questioning them in custody.
reading: In 1963, police in Phoenix, Arizona, arrested a man named Ernesto Miranda and questioned him for two hours. He signed a confession. No one had told him that he could refuse to answer or that he could have a lawyer. He was convicted. His lawyers argued that the confession violated the Fifth Amendment, because he had been pressured to be a witness against himself without knowing he could say no.

The Supreme Court agreed, five to four, in 1966. It ruled that before questioning a suspect who is in *custody*, meaning not free to leave, police must give a warning. The suspect must be told that they have the right to remain silent, that anything they say can be used against them in court, that they have the right to a lawyer, and that a lawyer will be provided if they cannot afford one. These are the *Miranda rights*, and you have heard them on every police show ever made.

Illinois helped set the stage. In 1964, two years before Miranda, the Court decided Escobedo v. Illinois, a case about a Chicago man who had asked to see his lawyer during questioning and been refused. The Court ruled the refusal was unconstitutional. Miranda took that idea and turned it into a clear rule that every officer could follow. Miranda himself was retried without the confession, convicted on other evidence, and served prison time.

Why does this matter for students? Under Illinois law, a young person under eighteen who is questioned by police about a serious crime has extra protections, including the right to have a lawyer present in some cases. The basic Miranda rule is simple to remember. If you are not free to leave, you may stay silent and ask for a lawyer, and asking cannot be used against you. Knowing that is not being difficult. It is being a citizen.

words.d: being held by police and not free to leave
the warnings police must give before questioning a suspect in custody, including the right to remain silent
a statement admitting to a crime

look.title: The Warning
look.text: The Court ruled that before any questioning, a person in custody must be warned that he has the right to remain silent, that anything he says can be used against him in court, that he has the right to have a lawyer present, and that if he cannot afford one, a lawyer will be appointed for him.
look.prompt: Each of these four warnings protects against a different danger. Name the danger each one is meant to prevent.

check.q: Why did the Supreme Court throw out Ernesto Miranda's confession?
choices: Because he was innocent
Because the police had no warrant
Because the trial was not public
Because he had not been told he could remain silent or have a lawyer
check.why: The Court ruled that questioning a suspect in custody without warning him of his rights violated the Fifth Amendment.

check.q: When must police give the Miranda warning?
choices: Before questioning a suspect who is in custody
Every time they speak to anyone
Only after a person is convicted
Only in cases involving a gun
check.why: The warning is required before questioning someone who is not free to leave, because that pressure is what the rule guards against.

check.q: How did an Illinois case help lead to Miranda?
choices: Illinois abolished confessions in 1960
Escobedo v. Illinois in 1964 ruled that refusing a suspect's request for a lawyer during questioning was unconstitutional
The Illinois Supreme Court wrote the Miranda warning
Miranda was arrested in Chicago
check.why: In Escobedo, a Chicago man had been denied his lawyer during questioning. The Court's ruling set the stage for the clear Miranda rule two years later.

lessons.title: Voting in Illinois
lessons.mainIdea: Voting in Illinois is easy to do and easy to skip, and the people who skip it still get governed.
reading: To vote in Illinois you must be a United States citizen, at least eighteen on election day, and a resident of your precinct for thirty days. You must *register*, which means putting your name on the official list of voters. You can register online, at the driver's license office, or even at the polls on election day. Illinois lets a seventeen-year-old vote in a primary election if they will be eighteen by the general election. Some of you can vote sooner than you think.

Illinois offers many ways to vote. You can vote early, for weeks before election day. You can vote by mail. You can vote in person on election day, when polls are open from six in the morning to seven at night. A *primary* is the election where each party picks its candidates. The *general election* is the one in November where the winners are chosen. Local elections for school boards and city councils are held in the spring of odd-numbered years, when few people are paying attention.

That last fact matters. In a presidential election, about two thirds of eligible Americans vote. In a midterm, when there is no president on the ballot, it drops to about half. In a spring school board election in Illinois, turnout is often below one in five. So the board that sets your school's calendar, budget and rules is usually chosen by a small group of mostly older voters. Whoever shows up decides.

Why do so many people skip it? Some say one vote cannot matter. Yet Illinois elections have been decided by a handful of votes, and some local races have been settled by a coin toss after a tie. Others say they do not know enough. That one is fixable, and the next lesson shows how. *Turnout*, the share of eligible people who actually vote, is the single number that decides who has power in a democracy.

words.d: to put your name on the official list of voters
an election in which a political party's voters choose its candidate
the election, usually in November, in which the final winners are chosen
the share of eligible people who actually vote

look.title: Who Shows Up
look.prompt: Turnout drops sharply when no president is on the ballot. What kinds of decisions are made in those lower-turnout elections, and who is making them?

check.q: Who may vote in an Illinois primary at age seventeen?
choices: Anyone seventeen with a driver's license
A seventeen-year-old who will be eighteen by the general election
No one under eighteen may vote in any election
Any high school senior
check.why: Illinois lets seventeen-year-olds vote in the primary if they turn eighteen by the general election.

check.q: When are most Illinois school board elections held?
choices: In November of presidential years
In November of every year
In the spring of odd-numbered years
In the summer
check.why: Local elections in Illinois are held in the spring of odd-numbered years, when turnout is often below one in five.

check.q: Why does low turnout in local elections matter?
choices: It makes elections cost more
It means the state must run the election again
It makes the results illegal
It means a small group of voters chooses the boards that run schools and cities
check.why: Whoever shows up decides. When few people vote, the school board that sets your calendar is chosen by a small, mostly older group.

lessons.title: Parties, Media and Finding the Truth
lessons.mainIdea: Parties and media help you sort information, but only checking sources tells you what is true.
reading: A *political party* is a group of people who join together to win elections and pass laws they agree on. The United States has two major parties, the Democrats and the Republicans, and several smaller ones. Illinois usually votes Democratic in statewide races, but many counties outside Chicago vote Republican, and the state has had governors from both parties. Parties are useful shortcuts. A label tells you roughly what a candidate believes. It also tempts you to stop thinking once you see the label.

The *media*, meaning newspapers, television, radio, websites and social media, is how most people learn about government. The First Amendment protects the press so it can report what officials would rather hide. A Chicago reporter's questions have sent more than one Illinois politician to prison. But anyone can publish today, and much of what spreads fastest online is wrong, either by mistake or on purpose. A video can be edited. A quote can be invented. A photo can be from another year and another country.

Professional fact-checkers use a habit called lateral reading. Instead of studying a page to decide if it looks trustworthy, they leave it and search for what others say about the source. Who runs this site? Who pays for it? Do other reliable sources report the same fact? A story that appears only in one place, has no named author, and makes you furious deserves extra suspicion. Anger is a signal that someone may be trying to use you.

Bias and lies are different problems. A newspaper can be biased, leaning one way in what it chooses to cover, while still reporting facts carefully. A post can be perfectly calm and completely false. Your job is to read sources from more than one side, notice what each leaves out, and check any surprising claim before you repeat it. In a democracy, the truth has no police. It has only citizens who bother to check.

words.d: a group of people who organize to win elections and pass laws they agree on
the ways news reaches people: newspapers, television, radio, websites and social media
checking a source by leaving the page to see what other reliable sources say about it
a lean toward one side in what is covered or how it is described

look.title: The Post That Made You Furious
look.text: A post says a new Illinois law will let the state read every student's text messages. It has a photo of the Capitol, a hundred thousand shares, and no link to the law. Your friend has already reposted it. You have three minutes before class.
look.prompt: List the three fastest checks you could do in those three minutes. What would convince you the post is true, and what would convince you it is false?

check.q: What is lateral reading?
choices: Reading a page from left to right slowly
Leaving a page to check what other sources say about it
Reading only sources from your own party
Reading a story twice before sharing
check.why: Fact-checkers do not stare at a page to judge it. They search for what reliable sources say about who is behind it.

check.q: Why does the First Amendment protect the press?
choices: So that all news stories will be unbiased
So newspapers can make more money
So reporters can expose what officials would rather hide
So the government can approve news before it prints
check.why: A free press can investigate the powerful. Chicago reporters' work has helped send Illinois politicians to prison.

check.q: What is the difference between bias and a lie?
choices: Bias is worse than a lie
Only social media can be biased
A biased source is always lying
A biased source leans one way but can still report facts, while a lie is false
check.why: Bias is about what gets covered and how. A lie is a false fact. A calm source can lie, and a leaning source can be accurate.

lessons.title: Ways to Take Part Now
lessons.mainIdea: You do not need to be eighteen to petition, speak at a meeting, serve, or argue well with someone who disagrees.
reading: The First Amendment's right to *petition* belongs to you today. A petition is a written request signed by many people. In Illinois, citizens can put some questions directly on the ballot by collecting signatures. Students have used petitions to get crosswalks, later start times and new classes. A petition with three hundred names from one school is hard for a board to ignore, because every name is a family.

Nearly every government meeting in Illinois is open to the public by law, and most have a time for *public comment*, when anyone can speak for a few minutes. School boards, city councils and park districts all hold them. Show up, sign in, and say your piece. Speak from a written note, name the problem, and ask for one specific thing. Board members remember the student who came in person far longer than they remember a hundred angry emails.

Student government is a real government in miniature: elections, a budget, and the same lessons about listening to people who did not vote for you. Service counts too. Illinois requires students to learn civics, and many districts count service hours. Volunteering at a food pantry, a library or a campaign teaches you how things actually get done. Illinois also lets sixteen-year-olds serve as election judges, the workers who run the polls on election day, with pay.

The hardest skill in this chapter is *civil discourse*: arguing with someone who disagrees without turning them into an enemy. Start by stating their view so well that they say yes, that is what I think. Ask what evidence would change their mind, and answer the same question yourself. Attack the idea, never the person. The framers built a system that only works if people who disagree can still share a country. That system is now yours to run.

words.d: a written request, signed by many people, asking a government to act
the part of a government meeting when any person can speak to the board or council
discussing disagreements respectfully, attacking ideas rather than people

look.title: Three Minutes at the Microphone
look.text: The school board meets Tuesday night. Item seven on the agenda is a plan to cut the late bus that lets students stay for clubs. Public comment is limited to three minutes per speaker. You have never spoken at a meeting. Twelve adults are there, mostly to talk about parking.
look.prompt: Write the first two sentences you would say. What one fact would you bring, and what one specific thing would you ask the board to do?

check.q: What is public comment?
choices: A time at a government meeting when anyone can speak
A newspaper's opinion page
A vote by the public on a law
A survey sent by the state
check.why: Illinois requires most government meetings to be open, and most include time for any person to address the board.

check.q: Which of these can a sixteen-year-old in Illinois legally do?
choices: Vote in a general election
Serve as a paid election judge at the polls
Run for the General Assembly
Sign a bill into law
check.why: Illinois allows sixteen-year-olds to work as election judges, the people who run polling places on election day.

check.q: Which behavior is part of civil discourse?
choices: Repeating your point louder
Refusing to talk to anyone who disagrees
Stating the other person's view so well that they agree you understood it
Pointing out the other person's flaws
check.why: Civil discourse means understanding the other view and attacking the idea, not the person.

review.q: Which amendment protects freedom of speech, the press and religion?
choices: The Fourth
The Fourteenth
The Fifth
The First
review.why: The First Amendment protects religion, speech, the press, assembly and petition.

review.q: What does the Fourth Amendment require before police search a home?
choices: Usually a warrant based on probable cause
Permission from the governor
A confession
A vote of the city council
review.why: Police normally need a warrant from a judge, backed by probable cause, to search a home.

review.q: Which amendment made everyone born in the United States a citizen and promised equal protection?
choices: The Thirteenth
The Fourteenth
The Fifteenth
The Nineteenth
review.why: The Fourteenth Amendment of 1868 defined citizenship and required states to give due process and equal protection.

review.q: What did the Nineteenth Amendment do?
choices: Ended slavery
Lowered the voting age to eighteen
Said the vote cannot be denied on account of sex
Created the Bill of Rights
review.why: Ratified in 1920, the Nineteenth Amendment barred denying the vote because of sex.

review.q: What rule did Tinker v. Des Moines set for schools?
choices: Schools may ban any political speech
Students have no free speech rights in school
Students may say anything at any time
Schools may limit student speech only if it substantially disrupts school
review.why: The Court protected the armbands and said schools need evidence of real disruption before limiting speech.

review.q: What did Brown v. Board of Education decide in 1954?
choices: That segregated public schools are unconstitutional
That separate but equal facilities are legal
That students must be given a lawyer
That the voting age is eighteen
review.why: The unanimous Court ruled that separate educational facilities are inherently unequal under the Fourteenth Amendment.

review.q: Which of these is required to vote in Illinois?
choices: Owning property
Being a citizen and at least eighteen on election day
Belonging to a political party
Passing a reading test
review.why: Illinois voters must be citizens, eighteen by election day, residents of their precinct for thirty days, and registered.

review.q: Why does a story that makes you furious deserve extra checking?
choices: Because angry stories are always false
Because the government bans angry stories
Because anger can be a sign someone is trying to use you, and checking sources takes only minutes
Because only calm stories are protected by the First Amendment
review.why: Posts designed to spread fast often aim at emotion. Lateral reading and checking other sources tells you whether the claim holds up.
